title: The Words Other Men Set to Music: Barbier, Carré, and the Paris of the Sung Legend
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rue de Bellefond and the First Stages

stops.name: Rue Marie-Éléonore-de-Bellefond, the painter's son is born
stops.date_confidence: attested, but the day is contradicted: fr.wikipedia gives 9 March 1825, en.wikipedia gives 8 March 1825, and neither cites a register. Not adjudicated
stops.campa: In a house at number 7, rue Marie-Éléonore-de-Bellefond, in the ninth arrondissement, a son is born to Nicolas Alexandre Barbier, painter and drawing professor, private secretary to the Duc d'Aumale, whose canvases King Louis-Philippe buys. The boy is a first cousin of Auguste Barbier, whose Iambes scald the July Monarchy in verse. He grows up between two trades: pictures made to order for a court, and poetry made against one. He will take neither. He will spend fifty years writing words for other men to set to music.
suggested_refs: The Paris état civil register of the 9th arrondissement, March 1825, which would settle the 8th against the 9th

stops.name: The Barbier household, the girl raised beside him
stops.date_confidence: attested for Lise Cristiani's birth, 4 December 1825; the relationship itself is contradicted between two articles of the same encyclopedia and is carried as reconstruction
stops.campa: A girl is brought up in the same household, born nine months after him: Agathe Barbier, who will take the stage name Lise Cristiani and become the first professional woman cellist in France and in Europe. The sources cannot agree what she is to him. One article calls her his niece of the same age. Another says she is an illegitimate child raised by the grandmother whose second husband is his own father, and that Jules considers her as his sister. She dies at twenty-seven in Novotcherkassk, in Russia, having played her way across Siberia. He never leaves Paris.
suggested_refs: Lise Cristiani's Siberian concert tour of 1849-1853 and the Stradivarius cello named after her

stops.name: Théâtre-Français, Amour et Bergerie
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month, day, cast or notice found in any consulted source, so the date defaults to 1 January
stops.campa: At twenty-three he puts a play on the first stage of France. Amour et Bergerie is given at the Théâtre-Français in the Palais-Royal, in the year the July Monarchy falls and the Second Republic is proclaimed. The consulted sources give the year and nothing else: no month, no cast, no notice of how it went. It is his oldest surviving credit, and it will still be his oldest surviving credit in 1890, when a claim goes round that Jeanne d'Arc holds that place. What he has not yet found is the collaborator, and the form.
suggested_refs: The registers of the Comédie-Française for the 1848 season

stops.name: Théâtre de l'Odéon, the tales of Hoffmann made into a play
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month or day found, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: With Michel Carré he assembles the tales of E.T.A. Hoffmann into one play, Les Contes fantastiques d'Hoffmann, and the Odéon stages it. The device is theirs: the drunken poet Hoffmann in a tavern, telling the loves of his own life as though they were his stories. Thirty years pass. Offenbach sees it, asks for it as an opera, and dies before the orchestration is done. A play written by two young men in 1851 becomes the frame of a dying composer's last work, and the only libretto Barbier will sign without Carré.
suggested_refs: The printed text of Les Contes fantastiques d'Hoffmann, Barbier and Carré, Odéon, 1851

stops.name: Paris, Galathée for Victor Massé
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month or day found, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Barbier and Carré write Galathée for Victor Massé, one of the first of the operatic collaborations that will run into the dozens. The method is fixed here and does not change: take a story the audience already knows, from Ovid or Molière or Goethe or Shakespeare, cut it to a length a singer can carry, hand it to whichever composer is asking. Pygmalion's statue wakes and turns out to be a nuisance. The pair are not inventing subjects. They are converting the literature of Europe into French singing parts, to order, at speed.
suggested_refs: Victor Massé's Galathée, opéra-comique in two acts, 1852

stops.name: Paris, Le Médecin malgré lui, the first Gounod
stops.date_confidence: year attested by fr.wikipedia; the day and venue are not in the verified pool. paul_barbier.journey.json in this same corpus asserts 15 January 1858 at the Théâtre-Lyrique, which is not independently confirmed and is not carried here
stops.campa: Their Molière reaches the stage with Gounod's music: Sganarelle, beaten into playing a doctor, curing by nonsense and growing rich by fraud. It is the first Barbier and Carré text Gounod sets that arrives before a public, and the rehearsal for what comes next. An American edition of the Faust libretto, printed nearly fifty years later, is careful to say where the credit for that next work belongs, and it does not assign it to the librettists. The comedy comes first; the tragedy is already being talked about in the same rooms.
stops.quote: But to the composer himself is due the credit of suggesting the story of Faust as a suitable subject for musical treatment.
stops.quote_source: Prefatory Note, Faust: A Lyric Drama in Five Acts, libretto by J. Barbier and M. Carre, music by Charles Gounod, Oliver Ditson Co. edition, 1906 (Project Gutenberg ebook 45806)
suggested_refs: Berlioz's notices in the Journal des débats for the 1858 season

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique, boulevard du Temple, Faust opens
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of March the Théâtre-Lyrique, housed since 1851 in the Théâtre Historique at 72 boulevard du Temple, gives Gounod's Faust with spoken dialogue between the numbers. The libretto is Barbier and Carré's, built on Carré's earlier play Faust et Marguerite and loosely on the first part of Goethe. The initial run succeeds and the publisher Choudens takes the work on tour. Mephistopheles enters in the first act dressed for the fashion, a sword at his side and a feather in his hat, and introduces himself.
stops.quote: Here am I! So, I surprise you? SATAN, Sir, at your service! A sword at my side; on my hat a gay feather;-- A cloak o'er my shoulder; and altogether, Why, gotten up quite in the fashion!
stops.quote_source: Mephistopheles' entrance, Act I, Faust: A Lyric Drama in Five Acts, English translation, Oliver Ditson Co. edition, 1906 (Project Gutenberg ebook 45806)
suggested_refs: The Théâtre Historique, 72 boulevard du Temple, home of the Théâtre-Lyrique 1851-1862; the site is now near 10 place de la République

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique, Marguerite at the casket
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere; the scene stands in Act III of the printed 1906 libretto
stops.campa: The libretto's centre of gravity is not the scholar and not the devil. It is Marguerite, who opens a casket left at her door, finds it full of jewels, puts them on, and cannot recognise the woman in the glass. From Goethe's enormous poem the two Frenchmen have taken the one thread a theatre can hold: a girl seduced, ruined, condemned, and at the last carried up. A German tragedy of knowledge becomes a French tragedy of a woman, and it runs on a mirror and a box of stones.
stops.quote: Ah! I laugh, as I pass, to look into a glass; Is it truly Marguerite, then? Is it you?
stops.quote_source: Marguerite's Jewel Song, Act III, Faust: A Lyric Drama in Five Acts, English translation, Oliver Ditson Co. edition, 1906 (Project Gutenberg ebook 45806)
suggested_refs: The Jewel Song, Ah! je ris de me voir si belle en ce miroir, Act III of Gounod's Faust

stops.name: Weimar, the desk the libretto is cut from
stops.date_confidence: facing stop, not a journey Barbier made. The pin is inherited byte-for-byte from goethe_full.journey.json; the date is the Paris premiere. Note that paul_barbier.journey.json pins its own Goethe-facing stop 65 km away at 51.4809, 11.972, which does not match Goethe's file
stops.campa: Goethe finishes the first part of Faust at Weimar. Johann Faust, the magician of the 1587 chapbook, never sets foot in Paris, the city where his story is eventually staged. Both lines end in a boulevard theatre, in French, sung. Goethe's own journey names Barbier from the other side, on Mignon. A prefatory note printed with the libretto in 1906 states which of the two Fausts the librettists actually adapted, and it is not the magician of the old books.
stops.quote: The love story with which the French librettists concerned themselves exclusively is wholly Goethe's conception, and finds no place in the old legends concerning the magician Faust. With true Gallic instinct they seized this pathetic episode as being best adapted for a lyric setting, and making the most potent appeal to the emotions of the spectators.
stops.quote_source: Prefatory Note, Faust: A Lyric Drama in Five Acts, Oliver Ditson Co. edition, 1906 (Project Gutenberg ebook 45806)
suggested_refs: Goethe's Faust, Part One, Tübingen, 1808

stops.name: Theater der Stadt, Baden-Baden, La Colombe
stops.date_confidence: attested. The verified pool hedged the place as Baden-Baden or Paris; the hedge is unnecessary, the Paris version is a separate premiere of 7 June 1866 at the Opéra-Comique
stops.campa: Gounod's La Colombe, one act to a Barbier and Carré text, opens not in Paris but at the Theater der Stadt in Baden-Baden, the German spa where Parisian money summers. It is played four times. Six years later a Paris version reaches the Opéra-Comique. In an itinerary otherwise made entirely of Paris addresses, Paris theatres and Paris graves, this is the only stop outside France, and no consulted source says whether the librettist crossed the Rhine to see it. The absence is a gap in the record, not a proof that he stayed home.
suggested_refs: The Baden-Baden summer seasons commissioned through Édouard Bénazet

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique, Philémon et Baucis
stops.date_confidence: year only, and the year itself rests on general operatic-history knowledge that was not re-verified this session. paul_barbier.journey.json gives 18 February 1860, unconfirmed in the verified pool
stops.campa: Gounod again, Ovid by way of La Fontaine, three acts by Barbier and Carré. Jupiter and Vulcan walk the earth disguised as tired travellers and are turned from every prosperous door until an old poor couple take them in and share what little they have. The gods give the two restored youth and a single death, and change them at the end into trees grown together. It is the Metamorphoses put on a lyric stage in the accent of the Second Empire. The pair are working now at the rate of a libretto a season.
sources: General operatic-history knowledge, flagged as unverified in the report
suggested_refs: Ovid, Metamorphoses VIII, and La Fontaine's Philémon et Baucis of 1685

stops.name: Paris, La Reine de Saba
stops.date_confidence: year attested by fr.wikipedia; no day given in the verified pool, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Barbier and Carré hand Gounod the queen who came out of the south to try Solomon with hard questions. The opera is a failure of the kind that does not stop a partnership: the pair have four more Gounod texts in them. What the libretto does is set a story from the other end of the Mediterranean on a Paris stage, by way of Nerval's own account of the East. Neither Sheba nor Solomon has been told that a Frenchman is putting their meeting to music, and neither of their journeys names him.
suggested_refs: Gérard de Nerval's Voyage en Orient, the immediate literary source of the Gounod opera's plot

stops.name: The Temple Mount, the meeting the opera stages
stops.date_confidence: facing stop, not a place Barbier went. The pin is the atlas canonical Temple Mount, inherited byte-for-byte; the date is the Paris premiere year
stops.campa: Sheba and Solomon meet at this stone, and the encounter is the thing both their own journeys turn on. Gounod's opera takes the same encounter and gives it a tenor architect, a jealous king and a fire in a foundry. The link runs one way only: neither Sheba's journey nor Solomon's mentions Gounod or Barbier, so the connection is thematic and not textual, and is recorded as reconstruction. A librettist in Paris is quarrying scripture the way he quarries Goethe.
suggested_refs: 1 Kings 10 and 2 Chronicles 9, the visit of the queen of Sheba

stops.name: Paris, Chevalier de la Légion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Forty years old, the state pins the cross on him. He has by now written Faust, and the Empire is beginning to understand what a librettist is worth to a country that exports its operas. Fifteen years will pass before the next grade. Between this decoration and that one he will write the Mignon, the Roméo et Juliette and the Hamlet that carry his name furthest, and bury the man he wrote nearly all of them with. The ribbon is given for work already done; the work that will be remembered is still ahead of him.
suggested_refs: The Légion d'honneur dossier of Jules Barbier, base Léonore, Archives nationales

stops.name: Salle Favart, Mignon
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.wikipedia's Salle Favart article gives the hall's coordinate as 48.8709, 2.3378, about 22 m from the pin used here
stops.campa: Ambroise Thomas sets their Wilhelm Meister at the Opéra-Comique, and the opera passes a hundred performances inside a year. Mignon is the stolen child who remembers a country of lemon trees she cannot name. Goethe's own journey looks forward to exactly this evening: the very Italy of his own longing, it says, which one day Barbier and Thomas will lift into opera. The hall itself has twenty-one years left. It burns in May 1887, and the third Salle Favart does not open on the site until 1898.
suggested_refs: Goethe, Wilhelm Meisters Lehrjahre, books III to VIII

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique Impérial du Châtelet, Roméo et Juliette
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Théâtre-Lyrique has moved to the Place du Châtelet, and Gounod's Shakespeare opens there while the Exposition Universelle fills Paris with foreign dignitaries who come to the run. Barbier and Carré string the play between four love duets and let the rest go: this is what a libretto does, and they have stopped apologising for it. Verona is remade for a French pit. The house that carries it will burn in the last week of the Commune four years later.
suggested_refs: The Théâtre-Lyrique on the Place du Châtelet, later rebuilt as the Théâtre de la Ville

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, Hamlet
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ambroise Thomas again, Shakespeare again, this time at the Opéra in the rue Le Peletier, with Jean-Baptiste Faure as Hamlet and Christine Nilsson as Ophélie. The libretto gives Ophélie a mad scene the play only reports, and gives the prince an ending the play does not have. Barbier and Carré write to the measure of the house. The Danish prince they hand the Opéra can hold a stage for four hours and leaves room for two great voices to do what the century pays to hear them do.
suggested_refs: The Salle Le Peletier, home of the Paris Opéra 1821-1873

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, Faust remade as grand opera
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no day given in the verified pool, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Ten years after the boulevard du Temple, Faust is rebuilt for the Opéra: the spoken dialogue is replaced throughout by sung recitative, and a ballet is added to the last act, because the Opéra requires one. In this form it becomes the most frequently performed opera in the house. The libretto Barbier and Carré wrote for a small theatre with actors who talk between the numbers is now a grand opera, and it is the version the nineteenth century means when it says Faust.
stops.quote: All hail, thou dwelling pure and lowly, Home of an angel fair and holy, All mortal beauty excelling!
stops.quote_source: Faust's aria (Salut! demeure chaste et pure), Act III, Faust: A Lyric Drama in Five Acts, English translation, Oliver Ditson Co. edition, 1906 (Project Gutenberg ebook 45806)
suggested_refs: The 1869 Paris Opéra recitative and ballet version of Faust

stops.name: Argenteuil, the death of Michel Carré
stops.date_confidence: attested as 27 June 1872 by en.wikipedia; paul_barbier.journey.json in this same corpus gives 28 June 1872, and the two are not reconciled here
stops.campa: The partner dies on the Seine at Argenteuil, in the suburb the painters are about to make famous. Twenty years of joint credits end: Molière, Goethe, Shakespeare, Corneille, Ovid, all of it signed by two men, most of it still in the repertory. Barbier is forty-seven and has thirty more years to work. He goes on being credited with Carré for another decade, on Paul et Virginie in 1876 and on Françoise de Rimini in 1882, and no source found explains whether those are old drafts or a house habit.
suggested_refs: The grave of Michel Carré at Argenteuil

stops.name: Théâtre de la Gaîté, Jeanne d'Arc
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month or day found, defaulted to 1 January. Which building on the Gaîté's shifting nineteenth-century footprint is meant is not confirmed by any consulted source
stops.campa: Two years after the Commune, Barbier writes his own drama on the maid of Lorraine and Gounod supplies the incidental music. The Third Republic wants a French subject that is not a defeat, and the librettist has one ready. It is his own text this time and not an adaptation of anybody, though the subject is the most adapted one in France. The play will come back in 1890 with Sarah Bernhardt in it, and even then it will not be the oldest thing he wrote.
suggested_refs: Gounod's incidental music to Jeanne d'Arc, 1873

stops.name: Domrémy, the girl the drama is about
stops.date_confidence: facing stop. The pin is inherited byte-for-byte from joan_of_arc.journey.json, its church of Saint-Rémy stop; the date is the Paris premiere year
stops.campa: Four hundred and forty years earlier, in this village on the Meuse, Joan of Arc heard voices in her father's garden and by the church of Saint-Rémy. Her own journey stops here and at Rouen, and does not mention Barbier, who never came. The traffic runs one way: a Paris librettist takes the most French of subjects, sets it for the stage of the Gaîté, and hands the Republic something to be consoled by. The connection is thematic and is recorded as reconstruction.
suggested_refs: The house of Jacques d'Arc and the church of Saint-Rémy at Domrémy

stops.name: Paris, Paul et Virginie for Victor Massé
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no day given in the verified pool, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Bernardin de Saint-Pierre's 1788 island novel becomes an opera for Victor Massé, and the bill still reads Barbier and Carré though Carré has been four years in the ground at Argenteuil. Whether the dead man's name stands because there are old drafts he really wrote, or simply because the pair are a brand the publishers will not break up, is not stated anywhere reachable. It is a gap, and it will open again in 1882 with a second posthumous credit.
suggested_refs: Bernardin de Saint-Pierre, Paul et Virginie, 1788

stops.name: Palais Garnier, Sylvia opens the new house's ballet
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Opéra has been in Garnier's building for a year, and the ballet that opens its repertory is Sylvia, ou la nymphe de Diane, scenario by Barbier and the Baron de Reinach, music by Léo Delibes, Rita Sangalli dancing, Louis Mérante choreographing. The librettist who has been feeding singers for twenty-four years now writes for dancers, in a house built to be looked at. There are no words in it at all. His trade turns out to be plot, and not verse.
suggested_refs: Tasso's Aminta, the pastoral behind the Sylvia scenario

stops.name: Théâtre de la Gaîté, Le Timbre d'argent at last
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Saint-Saëns finished this opera in 1865. Twelve years of the opera house's money troubles and one Franco-Prussian War stand between the score and an audience. It reaches the stage under Albert Vizentini's Théâtre National Lyrique at the Gaîté, conducted by Jules Danbé, to a Barbier and Carré libretto written when both authors were alive and both were younger men. A silver bell that pays out gold and kills each time it is struck: the pair wrote a second bargain opera after Faust, and it arrives twelve years after the composer laid down his pen.
suggested_refs: Saint-Saëns's Le timbre d'argent, composed 1864-1865, premiered 1877

stops.name: Palais Garnier, Polyeucte
stops.date_confidence: the year 1878 is attested by fr.wikipedia; the day 7 October and the Palais Garnier venue rest on general operatic-history knowledge and were not re-verified this session
stops.campa: Corneille's Armenian martyr, set by Gounod to a Barbier and Carré text. The subject is a Christian who breaks the idols and goes to his death for it, which is a strange thing to stage in the anticlerical Republic of 1878, and the opera does not last a season. Gounod has now had six of their libretti. Of the six, one is played everywhere on earth and the rest are played in France, and the librettist's name travels only on the back of the one that got out.
sources: General operatic-history knowledge, flagged as unverified in the report
suggested_refs: Corneille, Polyeucte martyr, 1643

stops.name: Paris, 10th arrondissement, the son who becomes Jean d'Yd
stops.date_confidence: birth date attested by fr.wikipedia, 'Jean d'Yd'; no street is given, so the coordinate is an approximate centre of the 10th arrondissement. The verified pool had wrongly pinned this at Jules Barbier's own birth address in the 9th
stops.campa: By the singer Berthe Perret, Barbier fathers a son who will act under the name Jean d'Yd and live until 1964, long enough to be filmed. His other son, Pierre Barbier, born 1854, is already becoming a librettist and writer in his turn. The mother of that first son is not named in anything reachable. Three generations of the family work the Paris theatre: a painter, a librettist, then a librettist and an actor. The wives and the mothers are mostly missing from the record.
suggested_refs: The filmography of Jean d'Yd, 1880-1964

stops.name: Paris, Officier de la Légion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Fifteen years after the chevalier's cross, the grade of officer, on the eve of the fourteenth of July. He is fifty-five. In October of this same year Offenbach will die with the orchestration of their opera unfinished, and in February of the next the work that carries Barbier's name alone will reach a stage. The Republic decorates him for the collaborations. What is coming is the one thing he did not share, and he has been carrying it since 1851.
suggested_refs: The Légion d'honneur dossier of Jules Barbier, base Léonore, Archives nationales

stops.name: Offenbach's residence, the abridged hearing
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the residence's exact address is not given in the verified pool, so the canonical Paris pin is used and the imprecision is stated here
stops.campa: An abridged private presentation of Les Contes d'Hoffmann is given at the composer's own house, with preliminary performers, before an invited room. Offenbach has about seventeen months to live. The frame is Barbier and Carré's from 1851: the poet drinking in a tavern while the students bang for beer, telling three loves that are three stories, none of which ends with him keeping the woman. The managers in the room are being asked to take the piece; the composer is asking against the clock.
stops.quote: Drig, drig, drig, master Luther, Spark of hades, Drig, drig, drig, for us more beer...
stops.quote_source: Students' opening chorus, Les Contes d'Hoffmann, English version by Charles Alfred Byrne, Charles E. Burden edition, New York, 1907 (Project Gutenberg ebook 15915). The English wording of this couplet was rendered by the tool that read the file and could not be cross-checked line by line
suggested_refs: Offenbach's Paris residence, 8 boulevard des Capucines, where the 1879 audition is placed by later accounts

stops.name: Paris, Offenbach dies with the orchestration unfinished
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The composer dies four months before the premiere, on the fifth of October. He leaves the piano score complete and the orchestration undone. Ernest Guiraud will finish it. The story that Offenbach died with the manuscript in his hand circulates widely and is not supported by the source consulted here, and is left out as an unverified deathbed flourish. What is attested is plainer and worse: a man of sixty-one finishes the notes and does not hear them played.
suggested_refs: Ernest Guiraud's completion of the orchestration, 1880-1881

stops.name: Salle Favart, Les Contes d'Hoffmann
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Thirty years after the Odéon play, the opera opens at the Opéra-Comique. It is the only libretto among the great ones that Barbier signs alone, Carré nine years dead. The Giulietta act is cut from this first production, and part of its music is moved into the Antonia act and the epilogue, which is how the Venice barcarolle survives while the Venice act does not. From this night the work exists in no fixed version. Editors will be arguing about it for a hundred and thirty years.
stops.quote: Belle nuit, o nuit d'amour, Souris a nos ivresses, Nuit plus douce que le jour, O belle nuit d'amour!
stops.quote_source: Barcarolle, Act III, Les Contes d'Hoffmann, French text, Charles E. Burden edition, New York, 1907 (Project Gutenberg ebook 15915)
suggested_refs: The second Salle Favart, home of the Opéra-Comique 1840-1887

stops.name: Salle Favart, the doll that sings
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere; the number stands in Act II of the Burden edition, whose Act I is the tavern prologue, correcting the verified pool's Act I attribution
stops.campa: In the act built out of Der Sandmann, the poet falls in love with Olympia and does not notice that she is a clockwork doll, because he is wearing glasses that were sold to him for the purpose. She sings her one song, runs down twice in the middle of it, and has to be wound. Hoffmann wrote the tale in 1816, the automaton's madness played straight; sixty-five years later Barbier and Offenbach turn the same clockwork bride into a coloratura aria and a stage joke, the horror kept just under the music.
stops.quote: Les oiseaux dans la charmille, Dans les cieux l'astre du jour, Tout parle a la jeune fille D'amour, d'amour
stops.quote_source: Olympia's Doll Song, Act II, Les Contes d'Hoffmann, French text, Charles E. Burden edition, New York, 1907 (Project Gutenberg ebook 15915), lines 4287-4290, speaker OLYMPIA (accompagne par Spalanzani)
suggested_refs: E.T.A. Hoffmann, Der Sandmann, 1816

stops.name: Salle Favart, the Muse has the last word
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere; the passage stands in the Epilogue of the Burden edition, lines 6574-6577, under the speaker heading LA MUSE (paraissant)
stops.campa: The three loves are lost, the poet is drunk on the tavern floor, and the Muse who has followed him all evening in a student's coat steps out and asks what she is: the faithful friend whose hand dried his eyes, through whom the grief he has been putting into women turns into work. It is the oldest bargain in the trade, set down by a man of fifty-six who has spent his whole life giving other people's stories to composers. He does not live to see the cut acts put back.
stops.quote: Et moi? Moi, la fidèle amie Dont la main essuya tes yeux? Par qui la douleur endormie S'exhale en rêve dans les cieux?
stops.quote_source: The Muse, Epilogue, Les Contes d'Hoffmann, French text, Charles E. Burden edition, New York, 1907 (Project Gutenberg ebook 15915), lines 6574-6577; two diacritics restored against the verified pool's transcription
suggested_refs: The epilogue of Les Contes d'Hoffmann in the Kaye-Keck critical edition

stops.name: Palais Garnier, Françoise de Rimini
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no day given in the verified pool, defaulted to 1 January. The Carré credit ten years after his death is unresolved in every consulted source and is not resolved here
stops.campa: Ambroise Thomas sets the second circle of the Inferno, and the bill again reads Barbier and Carré, ten years after Carré's death. Dante's own account of Paolo and Francesca has the poet hear the line about love absolving no one beloved from loving back, and fall down as a dead body falls, pity overtaking him mid-canto. Dante never knew of the opera; the opera does not know it is being read from the other end, six centuries later, in a different language, on a different kind of stage. Whether Carré wrote any of this is unresolved.
suggested_refs: Dante, Inferno V, 73-142

stops.name: Institut de France, the Académie candidacy
stops.date_confidence: the year of the candidacy is attested; no month or day given, defaulted to 1 January. The outcome beyond the bare fact of failure is a gap in the record
stops.campa: He stands for a seat under the dome on the quai de Conti. The sources confirm the candidacy and confirm that it comes to nothing. Who was elected instead they do not say, and no consulted source gives the vote. He is fifty-nine, has written the words of Faust, Mignon, Hamlet, Roméo et Juliette and Les Contes d'Hoffmann, and the Académie is not interested. The gap in the record is left as a gap, because closing it would take the Académie's own registers.
suggested_refs: The Académie française election registers for 1884

stops.name: Théâtre de la Porte-Saint-Martin, Sarah Bernhardt as Jeanne
stops.date_confidence: year attested, day not given, defaulted to 1 January. fr.wikipedia's Sarah Bernhardt article records her being injured during a performance of the Procès de Jeanne d'Arc at this theatre in 1890, which upgrades the verified pool's reconstruction to attested. The coordinate is corrected to 18 boulevard Saint-Martin
stops.campa: His Jeanne d'Arc returns to the boulevard with Sarah Bernhardt in the title part, seventeen years after the Gaîté. She is injured during one of the performances. Barbier is sixty-five and has been writing for the Paris stage since the year Louis-Philippe fled. A claim goes around that this is his oldest surviving text; it is not. Amour et Bergerie went up at the Théâtre-Français in 1848, twenty-five years before the maid of Lorraine, and the record is corrected here rather than repeated.
suggested_refs: The Théâtre de la Porte-Saint-Martin, 18 boulevard Saint-Martin

stops.name: Paris, the Dreyfusard
stops.date_confidence: the sources place his Dreyfusard activity in the 1890s without any date; 1894, the year of the first conviction, is used as an anchor and the imprecision is stated here rather than hidden
stops.campa: In the last years of his life the affair splits literary and artistic Paris, and Barbier takes the Dreyfusard side actively. No source reached names a petition he signed, an article he wrote, or a meeting he attended. What is attested is the position and nothing else, which is thin for a man of seventy, and is recorded here as thin rather than padded out. He has spent fifty years putting other people's convictions into other people's mouths. This one is recorded as his own.
suggested_refs: The lists of Dreyfusard signatories published in L'Aurore, January 1898

stops.name: Paris, 3rd arrondissement, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested by both fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia; no street address is given anywhere reached, and the coordinate is the approximate centre of the arrondissement
stops.campa: He dies in the third arrondissement at seventy-five, three weeks into the new century. Faust is by now the opera the nineteenth century played more than any other in its own great house; Les Contes d'Hoffmann is in no settled version and will not be for another hundred years. Neither source reached gives the street he died in, and the pin on this stop is the middle of an arrondissement. He is the author of words a great many people can sing from memory and almost nobody can attribute to anyone.
suggested_refs: The Paris death register of the 3rd arrondissement, January 1901

stops.name: Cimetière de Passy, the first grave
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Passy is attested; the exact date is given by no consulted source, and 19 January is a placeholder three days after the death
stops.campa: He is buried first at Passy, in the sixteenth, on the hill above the Trocadéro with the Eiffel Tower across the river. The cemetery is barely a hectare. It will not keep him. The verified pool carried a coordinate for this grave that fell some two hundred and forty metres outside the wall, which puts the tomb in a street it is not in. The corrected pin is the one the encyclopedia gives, and the error is written down in the report rather than quietly repaired.
suggested_refs: The Cimetière de Passy, 2 rue du Commandant-Schloesing

stops.name: Cimetière ancien de Châtenay-Malabry, the transfer
stops.date_confidence: the transfer from Passy is attested but no source gives its date, so the stop is filed at the year of death as a placeholder and sits out of chronological order for that reason
stops.campa: At some point nobody records, the remains are moved south out of Paris to the old cemetery of Châtenay-Malabry, on the avenue de la Division-Leclerc, where the tomb reads Famille Jules et Marie Barbier. Marie is a name on a stone and nothing more recoverable: no maiden name, no dates, no marriage. Paul Léautaud and Jean Fautrier lie in the same ground. Sully Prudhomme, whom the verified pool put here, died in this commune in 1907 and was buried at Père-Lachaise.
stops.quote: Auteur de la plupart des livrets des opéras de Charles Gounod dont Faust (1859), il collabora principalement avec Michel Carré. On lui doit également le livret des Contes d'Hoffmann (1881) de Jacques Offenbach.
stops.quote_source: French Wikipedia, article 'Jules Barbier', accessed 2026-08. An encyclopedic summary and not Barbier's own words; quoted as the sentence by which he is now chiefly described
suggested_refs: The tomb of the Famille Jules et Marie Barbier, 107 avenue de la Division-Leclerc, Châtenay-Malabry

stops.name: La Scala, Milan, Faust in Italian
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no day given, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: The opera goes abroad in translation. Milan hears it in Italian at La Scala; London hears it in Italian at Her Majesty's Theatre the following year. German houses have been playing it since 1861, and some of them do not call it Faust at all: they bill it as Margarethe, or as Gretchen, moving the title off the man who sells his soul and onto the girl who is sold. The librettists' choice of subject travels a great deal better than the librettists' own names do.
suggested_refs: The German performing tradition of Gounod's Faust under the title Margarethe

stops.name: London, an aria written in English and translated back
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no day given, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: For the English performances a new aria is composed to English words by Henry Chorley. Those words are then translated into French, and the result, Avant de quitter ces lieux, enters the French productions and stays there. A number written for London in a language neither author used becomes part of the standard Paris Faust. The libretto Barbier and Carré delivered in 1859 is no longer entirely the libretto that gets sung, and nobody thinks to ask them.
suggested_refs: Henry Fothergill Chorley's English text for Valentin's aria, 1864

stops.name: Saint-Mandé, twelve hundred and fifty pages in a house
stops.date_confidence: the decade is attested, the 1970s; no year, month or day is given by the source, so the date defaults to 1 January 1970. The verified pool recorded this as having no date at all, which was wrong
stops.campa: Antonio de Almeida finds roughly twelve hundred and fifty pages of Offenbach's manuscript at the Saint-Mandé house of an heir of one of the composer's daughters: vocal scores, fragments of the libretto, and Guiraud's orchestration of the Venice act that was cut in 1881. It has been sitting in a family house on the eastern edge of Paris for the better part of ninety years. Fritz Oeser's edition follows in 1976 and Michael Kaye's in 1988, both of them fed by the find.
suggested_refs: The Almeida manuscripts of Les Contes d'Hoffmann, recovered at Saint-Mandé

stops.name: Paris, the heroine restored to one voice
stops.date_confidence: the edition's year is attested; no month or day, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: The Kaye-Keck edition reconciles a century of manuscript work and presents what it argues was the original dramatic conception: one soprano across all the acts and one baritone against her, so that the three lost loves are one woman and the three men who take them away are one man. Barbier's 1851 frame is at last read as it was written. He has been dead a hundred and ten years, and the libretto is still being edited toward what somebody believes it meant.
suggested_refs: The Kaye-Keck critical edition of Les Contes d'Hoffmann, 2011
